Q10: Some studies would extract means of a given variable (arm-based meta-analysis), or effect sizes that were already calculated in primary studies. In the former, there is no formula needed and it is not technically an "effect size" sensu stricto; and in the latter, the effect sizes are already available and the formulas are likely in the original studies (and may vary between studies). I think it is relevant to have an "NA" category here for these cases.
Q12: The authors almost always report the type of model they use, but the details of the model specifications are often unclear. For instance, some authors would state that they used a "random-effect model" only when "they found heterogeneity". Identifying which model is fixed or random is thus unclear and not transparent. It is also almost always unclear what random effect is used. I get that the definition of a "random-effect" model is clear for most people (i.e., study-level random effect), but I think this item would be more interesting if authors clearly reported which random effects were used, particularly for multi-level models.
Q14: I was a bit confused about the wording of this item. It is quite common for authors to report the % of weights taken by each study in their analyses, but not how these weights were calculated, or even how the sampling variance of the effect size was calculated. Also, what if authors say they used an "inverse-variance model", but do not provide the formula for calculating the sampling variance? How about cases where authors say they used a specific package (e.g., metafor) that automatically calculates sampling variance? I think this question needs to be very specific about what counts as "yes" or "no".
Q16:
This was a tricky one too. If the authors used a random-effect model, then in almost all cases it is to account for the non-independence of effect sizes among studies, but the authors do not necessarily mention non-independence directly. Also, what about cases when authors say that they extracted multiple effect sizes per study, but don't do anything about it? Or what if they say that they used a random-effect model because they extracted multiple effect sizes per study, but don't say that this generates a source of non-independence? 
I think it would be relevant to require people to statistically account for effect size dependence, not just "mention" non-independence.
Q18: I found that many studies do not have an "overall effect", because it is not necessarily relevant to their questions. Then it is really hard to determine what is an "overall mean-effect" for the "meta-regression". What if the authors did a variety of meta-regressions but it does not seem that one stands out as the "overall" or "main" objective? I think it will be hard to apply this item for some studies. Maybe one solution would be to have an "NA" category for studies that do not have an "overall" aim?
Q20: I found that authors sometimes mention that they assessed heterogeneity, but do not necessarily report the values of their heterogeneity assessment. What response should be used in this case? I also found a case where they only reported I2 for a small subgroup analysis in the supplement, but not for the main models. Does this count as "yes" or "no"? I think we can be a bit more strict here, and require people to report heterogeneity values for their main analyses.
Q26: I think it's worth noting that the data availability statement is sometimes only displayed in the online html version (not in the PDF). Also, what is referred to as "the data" needs to be more strictly defined as "raw data". It is very common for authors to present some data, or the data with the calculated effect sizes, but not the RAW data that was used to calculate the effect sizes.
Q30:
I think the tool is pretty easy to use overall, but it would be helpful to have more examples or a small FAQ for each question. The description of each item is quite short and it leaves some gaps for interpretation. 
For instance, items 10-12 say that authors have to "report" publication bias/heterogeneity/sensitivity analyses. What if the authors say they did, but don't report the results of these assessments? What if the authors' objective is not to calculate an overall effect because it hardly makes sense for their study in Item 9?
I really think a more thorough description of each item + a FAQ could help answer most questions people would have, and ensure the tool is fully reproducible. 
I also think that Item 6 is too vague, because the type of model does not tell much about the actual model structure. At the end of the day, I see this tool not just as an assessment of already published studies, but also as a guide people can use to design and report their study. If people see that only suggesting the model type is proposed in this tool, then it suggests it is part of best/recommended practices. However, this is clearly not enough in practice, and I think making the tool stricter overall (e.g., recommending reporting the whole model specification)can really push forward practices and make sure people report things more thoroughly.
